x1<- (1:N - 0.5)/N
w<- (1:N)*sqrt(2.)
x2<- w - trunc(w)

Now x1 and x2 are the 2-D quasirandom sequence you need.

messages.body_plain:
Sorry: This wasn't a real Halton sequence, as the sqrt(2) sequence is 
not the right way to do this (it should really be a reflection of the 
base-2 number instead).

However, the 2-D sequence as given is still a quasirandom sequence.

To generate real Halton or Hammersley sequences would require 
somewhat more programming.

A very good set of 2-D quasirandom low discrepancy numbers is

F3<- 1
F2<- 1
for (i in 1:?) {
   F1<- F2 + F3
}
x1<- 1:F1/F1
w<- (1:F1)*F3/F1
x2<- w - trunc(w)

i.e., the F's are the Fibonacci sequence.

On Wed, Jun 09, 2010 at 11:02:03AM -0400, Crawford. Winnie wrote:

> I've looked for the equation S-Plus uses in predict() for multiple
> discriminant analysis so I can duplicate the results in Excel, but
> have had no luck. The function discrim() outputs the group means,
> covariance matrices, constants for each group, and a linear
> coefficient matrix for each group and K dimension. I have 2 groups and
> K=2, so the matrices are 2 X 2. Predict() outputs the probability that
> a record of the 2 variables belongs to one group or the other. I'd
> like to know the form of the equation that outputs those
> probabilities. Can anyone point me in the right direction? Thanks.

You can see the code for prediction from discrim() by looking at
the predict.discrim() function.  It is all done in S code, no C
or Fortran.

Here is an example of the default predictions with 2 groups and
3 random predictors:

# make up some data:
mydf <- data.frame(x1 = runif(30), x2 = runif(30), x3 = runif(30),
    y = sample(letters[1:2], 30, rep=TRUE))

# discrim opbject:
d1 <- discrim(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = mydf)

# predictions:
p1 <- predict(d1, new = mydf)

# predictions by "hand"
xmat <- as.matrix(mydf[, -4])
cmat <- coef(d1)$linear.coefficients
dist <- scale(xmat %*% cmat,  -coef(d1)$constants, F)
# scale the distances:
dist <- exp((dist - rowMaxs(dist)))
dist <- dist/rowSums(dist)

# round like predict.discrim:
dist <- round(dist, options()$digits)

# check with the predict() results:
p1[,-1] - dist

-Stephen Kaluzny

After I sent out my note on how to compute predictions by "hand" for a
linear discriminant function, a user asked:

  How would the process work with a quadratic discriminant, such as the
  one used as an example in the help file?

Here is an example of computing the predictions using the quadratic
discriminant function example from the discrim() help file:

iris.quad <- discrim(Species ~ Sepal.Length + Sepal.Width +
    Petal.Length + Petal.Width, data=iris.df, family=Classical("heter"))

# predictions:

# predictions by "hand" following computations in predict.discrim:

    function(w, x) rowSums(x %*% w * x), x)))

# scale the distances:
dist <- exp((dist - rowMaxs(dist)))
dist <- dist/rowSums(dist)

Bernd,

Given the error message of "Permission Denied", I'd guess that your user
account does not have permission to delete files in the directory C:\Program
Files\Insightful\SPlus6.2\users\(your user name). This can occur when S-Plus
is installed using an Administrator account---the Administrator has full
access to the entire directory tree, but a regular user does not, and thus
cannot create/delete files.

Try logging into your machine as Administrator (or contact your
Administrator if you do not have access) and giving full access permissions
to your user account for your user directory C:\Program
Files\Insightful\SPlus6.2\users\(your user name).

HTH,

Chris Green

messages.body_plain:
Greeting Listserv Readers,

At http://r4stats.com/popularity I have added plots, data, and/or
discussion of:

1. Scholarly impact of each package across the years
2. The number of subscribers to some of the listservs
3. How popular each package is among Google searches across the years
4. Survey results from a Rexer Analytics poll
5. Survey results from a KDnuggests poll
6. A rudimentary analysis of the software skills that employers are
seeking

Thanks very much to all the folks who helped on this project including:
John Fox, Marc Schwartz, Duncan Murdoch, Martin Weiss, John (Jiangtang)
HU, Andre Wielki, Kjetil Halvorsen, Dario Solari, Joris Meys, Keo
Ormsby, Karl Rexer, and Gregory Piatetsky-Shapiro.

If anyone can think of other angles, please let me know.

Cheers,
Bob
